#10283. On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery

Today, we are introducing on-device Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities in Google AI Edge Gallery. Voice is often the most natural way to interact with AI on phones and wearables. Recent advances in compact speech architectures now make it possible to run accurate, multilingual ASR and expressive TTS models entirely on device, all within a small memory footprint, with low latency, and completely offline. By pairing these lightweight speech models with on-device small language models (SLMs) like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4, developers can build apps that stream live transcriptions as the user speaks and synthesize natural spoken replies locally.

This release brings together major advancements across both Google’s system speech models and the open-weight ecosystem:

Below, we’ll explore how this local voice pipeline powers the new XR (Extended Reality) Language Teacher showcase, upgrades AI Chat in Google AI Edge Gallery, and how you can build with these APIs and models today.

Learning a language while traveling happens in the real world, often in underground stations, busy markets, or abroad where Wi-Fi and roaming data may not be available. To show how vision, language, and speech models can work together 100% locally on your phone with no network connection needed, we built the XR Language Teacher showcase in Google AI Edge Gallery. Simply point your camera at an unfamiliar object or menu, ask "What is that, and how do I ask for one?", and immediately hear an explanation in your language alongside authentic pronunciation in the local language.

Link to Youtube Video (visible only when JS is disabled)

With inference running locally on a paired phone, the same experience works standalone on a phone and extends naturally to hands-free smart glasses. To see how we adapted Language Teacher for intelligent glasses check out our recent talk at Android Dev Summit: Building Audio-First Experiences for Intelligent Eyewear with Gemini Nano.

Beyond the XR Language Teacher showcase, we also built ASR and TTS directly into Google AI Edge Gallery’s main AI Chat feature, giving on-device SLMs like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 a natural, offline voice interface while on the go.

Link to Youtube Video (visible only when JS is disabled)

While multimodal models like Gemma 4 can process audio inputs directly, we provide a modular solution for cascading language models with separate, lightweight voice models for latency optimization and flexibility. Depending on your target devices and model requirements, our open-source code on GitHub shows you the optimized and recommended solution for Android using ML Kit, as well as MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform coverage and open model support.

For developers building for Android devices, ML Kit’s GenAI Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech APIs provide a standardized, platform-integrated path out of the box. With the underlying speech models managed through AICore and Google’s on-device speech services, developers get production-grade quality without having to manage model downloads or worry about APK size bloat. Your app also benefits automatically from hardware acceleration across NPU and TPU backends (when available) and seamless background model updates.

Integrating ASR and TTS into cross-platform applications usually requires handling low-level audio framing, Voice Activity Detection (VAD), and complex decoding pipelines. MediaPipe Task simplifies this by providing unified, turnkey ASR and TTS APIs across iOS, macOS, Windows, Linux, and Web that abstract away manual pre-processing, audio stream routing, and platform-specific audio management into simple, high-level interfaces:

Under the hood, ML Kit and MediaPipe Tasks are powered by LiteRT, Google’s high-performance on-device AI inference infrastructure. Cross-platform applications requiring even more fine-grained control over speech processing or custom model architectures can also build on it directly.

Speech models often rely on multiple subgraphs and auxiliary assets, such as encoder/decoder subgraphs and tokenizers for ASR, or phonemizer dictionaries, voice embeddings, and vocoders for TTS. All required components for each model are packaged into a single .litertlm file for easy deployment. The app ships with ready-to-use .litertlm models, including Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 (multilingual ASR), PocketTTS 100M (multilingual TTS), Phonon 31M (ultra-lightweight English TTS), and Kokoro-82M (multilingual TTS). Beyond these, the vibrant Hugging Face LiteRT Community with over 10K+ followers offers a growing catalog of open-weight models, like Whisper, Qwen3-ASR and Moonshine for ASR, or Qwen3-TTS and Matcha for TTS. For developers seeking custom implementations or support for additional open-weight voice models, LiteRT provides a rich set of multimodal model examples to help you get started, with more on the way.

Adding a local voice pipeline takes on-device SLMs beyond typing-based chat interfaces, enabling natural, voice-first interactions that work anywhere, completely offline. All the building blocks to try these experiences or integrate them into your own apps are available today:

We'd like to extend a special thanks to our significant contributors for their work on this project:

Alice Zheng, Ajay Dudani, Alex Kanaukou, Amy Zeppenfeld, Byungchul Kim, Cheng Yang, Chintan Parikh, Chris Parsons, Cormac Brick, David Chou, Dong Chen, Geonsun Lee, Glenn Cameron, Hriday Chhabria, Ian Ballantyne, Ireneu Pla, James O’Donnell, Jamieson Pryor, Jason Poon, Jenn Lee, Jianing Wei, Jing Jin, Jingxiao Zheng, Jingyu Shi, Karthik Thirumalai, Kristen Wright, Lu Wang, Marius Kintel, Matthias Grundmann, Miao Wang, Mogan Shieh, Na Li, Paul Hsia, Qiumin Xu, Ravi Shankar, Rishika Sinha, Ronald Wotzlaw, Sachin Kotwani, Sandeep Patil, Sebastian Schmidt, Shao-Fu Shih, Shuangfeng Li, Suril Shah, Tiger Souvannakoumane, Tzu-Ping Chen, Weiyi Wang, Wentao Tu, Yang Yang, Yi-Chun Kuo, Yishuang Pang, Yu-che Liu, Yu-hui Chen, Yuling Liang, Zhihao Yang, Zichuan Wei.

#10282. Google Maps might change its colors again, but it’s optional this time [Gallery]

Google Maps has a pretty consistent style, but a new option appears to be in the works with a darker “high-visibility” setting.

The last major change to Google Maps styling came in 2023 (yes, time flies) when the platform rolled out a new color palette to all users. This was divisive among users, but ultimately worked out.

Now, Google appears to be working on another new shake-up.

The folks over at Android Authority spotted a new “high-visibility” toggle in the latest Google Maps update for Android, with the new style having darker colors for the map in both light and dark modes, as well as a purple line for your route compared to the blue we’re used to seeing.

The change was also spotted on Android Auto, with much darker colors (including a near-black dark mode) in both color settings for your car’s display. This is likely tied to this new “High-visibility” setting, but it’s hard to say for certain – teardowns and enabling new features early can only tell us so much.

This appears to all be controlled by a new “Map style” setting in Google Maps, with “Standard” and “High-visibility” settings available. Functionally, everything remains the same, it’s just a new set of colors.

So, where the previous color changes were forced on all users, this one is at least optional, and the “High-visibility” naming seems like it’s targeted at those with difficulties in sight more so than just a general change for all users.

#10279. Hands-on: Sony’s Walkman-revival USB-C headphones are back in stock and worth a look

Sony’s iconic Walkman headphones are back in the USB-C MDR-3R and, after quickly selling out on launch day, they’ve now been restocked. And, after using them, I can see why they sold out so quickly.

The MDR-3R are Sony’s revival of the wired over-ear headphones that many used with a classic Walkman player. The retro style still looks great in 2026, but using an original pair is a bit of a headache in today’s age of headphone jack-less smartphones. So it was nice to see Sony give this a revival with USB-C.

Update 11/24: After we first published our hands-on with MDR-3R last week, Sony’s USB-C headphones sold out pretty quickly again. As of today, though, they’re back in stock and still shipping in early December – don’t miss out!

While the style won’t be for everyone, I think these work brilliantly. The sound quality is excellent and having a pair of headphones that doesn’t fully enclose my ears is pretty refreshing. There’s no noise cancellation, but with open-ear earbuds becoming more popular, I actually really like these as a similar solution (though high volumes will definitely be heard by those around you). I’m not fully cut off from the world around me, but I’m also able to get good sound quality. Lows are the weakness here, with unimpressive bass drops, but the sound quality is crisp and clear and pretty neutral, and the open-ish style makes it feel like the room around me is filled with music.

The physical hardware is great. While a plastic and metal build is objectively not as comfy as a premium pair of ANC headphones, the extremely light weight helps MDR-3R become an afterthought. You simply forget you’re wearing them after a few minutes.

The earpads are swappable, with orange and blue options included in the box.

As for the USB-C cable, it’s fully plug-and-play. No app needed and it worked across every device I tested (including Pixel, which doesn’t work with all USB-C audio output). I do wish the cable was perhaps a few inches longer, but it’s long enough to wear the headphones with my phone in my front pocket. There’s a remote along the cable for play/pause and volume adjustments, though I think it’s a little too high on the cable.

For $59.99, these are a fun pair of USB-C headphones to have on hand. They sound good, work great, and don’t cost an arm and a leg. I can see why they sold out so quickly on launch day – in just 10 hours, Sony told me.

Sony MDR-3R are back in stock now and shipping in early December. If you want a pair, I say don’t wait. They’re well worth at least trying if you can get them for retail price – please don’t give in to the scalpers selling these at double, they’re not worth that.

Follow Ben: Twitter/X, Threads, Bluesky, and Instagram

Razer, the brand best-known for its gaming peripherals and laptops, has another quirky collaboration. This time around, the Singapore-American company managed to squeeze in a partnership with Durex for a limited-edition pack of a Razer Goliath mousepad with two Razer-branded Durex Performa delay condoms.

Work hard, game harder - Razer x Durex (China exclusive) https://t.co/3iPBFRQGyFNovember 24, 2026

Before everyone gets too excited, this partnership is specific to the China region. Prospective gamers hoping for a bit of extra after-match fun can reportedly get their hands on the package in two ways: as post-purchase gifts at the Razer or Durex stores on JD.com, or at Tmall's Durex store via redeeming points or as a special offer during live-stream events. There will also be a giveaway held on Dec. 7, though no further details were provided.

There's a lot of inter-cultural play in this promotion, as the Goliathus mouse pad is named Heavy Armored Beetle in China (重装甲虫), while the specific Durex condom variant is 持久战甲, roughly "long-lasting battle armor," or protection — plus, both contain the armor/shell symbol 甲. The doubles fun continues with "DLS", as it can be read as "take Razer" (Dài Léishé) or the local pronunciation of Durex, Dùlěisī. The partnership's slogan is "for gaming, bring Razer; for romance, bring Durex."

遂にゲーミングコンドーム登場 RazerとDurexがまさかのコラボらしい ※中国限定 https://t.co/k6gY1k10SSOctober 23, 2026

Razer and Durex may stand out as quite the odd couple, but the condom maker has been a sponsor of the Chinese League of Legends Pro League since 2023. Meanwhile, Razer is no stranger to quirky collaborations, as we've seen Razer Gillette razors, Razer-Panerai watches, sneakers, pickleball paddles, Dolce & Gabbana-branded headsets, and even tea. The younger Chinese demographic is reportedly more open to this type of initiative, with unconventional branding pairings having good market uptake.

Online commenters were quick to exercise their proverbial mouths, questioning if the target gamer demographics would have a use for the condoms to begin with, and some suggested the decision to offer only two per pack was probably wise. Some outlets were cracking jokes about RGB lighting on the rubbers, too.

#10276. Your AI Pipeline Works. But Can You Trust It?

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI is becoming a part of almost everything we do in technology today. Whether it's detecting fraudulent transactions, assessing credit risk, forecasting demand, or personalizing customer experiences, organizations are increasingly relying on AI to make faster and smarter decisions.

And naturally, when we talk about building AI systems, most of the conversation revolves around model accuracy, performance, and deployment. We spend considerable time making sure our models are trained well, our pipelines run efficiently, and our systems can handle production workloads.

But here's something we don't always pay enough attention to: Can we actually trust the data feeding these models?

After all, even the most sophisticated AI model can produce misleading results if the underlying data is incomplete, inconsistent, or incorrectly interpreted. What's interesting is that these problems don't always show up as technical failures. Sometimes, everything appears to be working perfectly fine.

Imagine a financial institution that has recently deployed an AI-powered loan risk assessment system. The team has spent months preparing the data, training the model, testing its performance, and finally moving it into production.

The deployment goes smoothly. Data pipelines are running on schedule, predictions are being generated, and all the monitoring dashboards are green.

A few weeks later, however, the business team notices something unusual. The model has started classifying more customers as high risk than expected.

The data science team checks the model configuration. Nothing has changed. The engineering team reviews the pipelines. All jobs have completed successfully. Even the infrastructure looks healthy.

It turns out that an upstream source system changed the definition of a customer income field from annual gross income to annual net income. The field name remained the same, the data type was still numeric, and none of the existing technical validations detected the change.

The pipeline continued running as expected, but the model was now receiving information with a different business meaning.

This brings us to an important point: Just because an AI pipeline runs successfully doesn't necessarily mean we can trust its output.

Building reliable AI systems requires us to look beyond the model itself. We need to understand where the data originates, how it changes as it moves through different systems, whether it meets quality expectations, and who is responsible when something goes wrong.

In this article, we'll explore three important elements of trustworthy AI pipelines (data quality, data lineage, and accountability) and look at how engineering teams can incorporate them into their existing workflows without making the process unnecessarily complicated.

Most modern data pipelines come with some form of operational monitoring. Engineering teams track job completion, execution time, system availability, and processing failures.

These metrics are important because they help us understand whether our systems are functioning as expected.

Operational monitoring primarily tells us whether a pipeline executed successfully. It doesn't necessarily tell us whether the data being processed is accurate, consistent, or suitable for the model consuming it.

Suppose we're building a loan risk model that uses a customer's debt-to-income ratio as one of its input features.

Debt-to-income ratio = Monthly debt payments / Monthly income

Now imagine that an upstream system starts supplying annual income instead of monthly income.

The calculation still executes successfully. The values are numeric, the transformation doesn't throw an error, and the model continues generating predictions.

However, the resulting debt-to-income ratio is incorrect because the numerator and denominator represent different time periods.

This is where traditional monitoring falls short.

To build trustworthy AI pipelines, we need to look at different dimensions of system health.

A pipeline can be operationally healthy while processing unreliable data. Similarly, a model can continue producing predictions even when the meaning of an important input field has changed.

For engineering teams, the objective should be to identify these problems as early as possible, ideally before they reach downstream models.

We've all heard the phrase "garbage in, garbage out."

And despite all the progress we've made in artificial intelligence, this principle hasn't changed.

AI models may be capable of processing enormous volumes of data and identifying complex patterns, but they cannot automatically guarantee that the information they're receiving is correct.

This is where data quality becomes important.

Data quality refers to how well information meets the requirements of its intended use. In AI pipelines, it helps us determine whether incoming data is sufficiently reliable for model training, evaluation, or inference.

Let's look at four dimensions that are particularly relevant.

Imagine we're developing a loan risk model that relies on customer income, outstanding debt, repayment history, and credit utilization.

What happens if 20% of the incoming records are missing income information?

Should we reject those records? Should we replace missing values using an approved statistical method? Or should we flag them for additional review?

There isn't one answer that works for every system.

The right approach depends on the model, the business requirements, and the potential consequences of the decision.

What matters is that missing information is handled deliberately.

For example, replacing missing income with zero may allow the pipeline to continue running, but it could significantly distort the model's predictions.

Validity checks whether values meet expected formats, ranges, and business rules.

Consider a customer record containing the following information:

The credit utilization value immediately stands out.

Although credit utilization can exceed 100% in certain circumstances, a value of 450% may warrant investigation.

This highlights an important distinction: Not every unusual value is incorrect, and not every technically valid value is meaningful.

A database may accept any numeric value, but the business may need additional rules to determine whether that value is appropriate for the model.

Engineering teams should distinguish between invalid records, unexpected observations, and legitimate exceptions.

This is one of the most common challenges in enterprise data environments.

Imagine two systems providing customer income information.

Both datasets contain a column called income.

If we combine these datasets without understanding their definitions, we risk introducing inconsistencies into downstream calculations.

The data may look perfectly fine from a technical perspective. The problem is that the same field represents different business concepts.

This is why data definitions, units, and transformation rules are just as important as schema validation.

Suppose a model predicts a customer's current financial risk using income information that was last updated 18 months ago.

The data might be accurate, complete, and consistent.

But is it current enough to support the decision?

Different AI applications have different freshness requirements.

A real-time fraud detection model may require near-real-time transaction information, while a long-term forecasting model may work with less frequently updated datasets.

The important thing is to define these expectations based on how the data will be used.

The good news is that improving data quality doesn't always require sophisticated enterprise tools.

A practical starting point is to define validation rules for the most important input fields.

For example, consider the following conceptual configuration:

This is an illustrative data quality contract rather than executable configuration for a particular framework.

It defines basic expectations and specifies what should happen when the data fails validation.

Tools such as Great Expectations can help automate these checks. For smaller systems, custom SQL or Python validations may be sufficient.

However, technical validation alone isn't enough.

Remember our original example where the income field changed from gross to net income?

Both values could easily pass a rule requiring income to be greater than zero.

Detecting that kind of issue requires clear business definitions, communication with upstream systems, and appropriate change management.

In other words, data quality isn't just about checking values. It's also about understanding what those values represent.

Now let's assume our loan risk model generates an unexpectedly high risk score for a customer.

The model output is available, but we want to understand what contributed to the prediction.

The income information came from a customer application system. Outstanding debt came from another database. Both datasets went through several transformations before reaching the feature engineering pipeline.

The final features were then passed to the model.

At this point, a seemingly simple question becomes surprisingly difficult:

Where exactly did the information used for this prediction come from?

This is where data lineage becomes valuable.

Data lineage describes how data originates, moves, and changes across different systems.

For AI pipelines, it helps us understand the journey from raw source data to the features used by a model.

Source Systems → Data Transformation → Feature Engineering → Model Inference → Predictions

Each stage introduces dependencies that can affect downstream results.

Data lineage can be captured at different levels of detail.

Dataset-level lineage shows relationships between datasets.

Loan Applications → Cleaned Applications → Model Features

This helps us understand how datasets move through the overall architecture.

However, suppose the model's debt-to-income ratio suddenly changes.

Dataset-level lineage might tell us which datasets were involved, but it may not provide enough detail to identify the affected field.

That's where column-level lineage becomes useful.

debt_to_income_ratio = monthly_debt_payment / monthly_income

Column-level lineage can show that the resulting feature depends on two upstream attributes.

If one of those attributes changes, engineers can trace the dependency and investigate the impact.

This is especially valuable in environments where multiple reports, applications, and AI models depend on shared data sources.

Large organizations may use dedicated metadata management and lineage platforms.

However, smaller teams can start by capturing essential metadata during pipeline execution.

OpenLineage provides an open standard for collecting and exchanging lineage metadata across supported systems.

It's important to understand that lineage doesn't automatically guarantee data accuracy.

A pipeline can be perfectly documented and still contain incorrect transformation logic.

But when something goes wrong, lineage gives engineering teams a clearer starting point for investigation.

Instead of searching across multiple systems and trying to reconstruct dependencies manually, they can identify where data originated and how it changed along the way.

An AI model starts producing unexpected results.

The data science team checks the model and finds no issues.

The data engineering team confirms that the pipelines are running successfully.

The source-system team verifies that data was delivered according to its interface.

Everyone has completed their individual checks, but nobody has identified who should coordinate the investigation.

This is where accountability becomes important.

AI pipelines often involve multiple teams responsible for different stages of the data lifecycle. Without clearly defined ownership, even relatively simple issues can take longer to resolve.

A practical accountability framework should distinguish between three responsibilities.

Data owners are responsible for defining the business meaning and expected quality of critical information.

For example, someone needs to determine whether an income field represents gross income, net income, or another financial measure.

These definitions should be documented and communicated to downstream consumers.

Data engineering and platform teams typically manage data ingestion, transformations, validation mechanisms, and pipeline operations.

Their responsibilities may include implementing quality checks, monitoring failures, and assessing the technical impact of changes.

However, technical teams shouldn't be expected to make business-definition decisions without appropriate input.

Data science and ML engineering teams are responsible for evaluating model behavior, managing model versions, and assessing how changes in input data may affect predictions.

If a critical feature changes, the model team may need to determine whether additional testing, recalibration, or retraining is required.

Defining ownership is useful, but connecting it to an operational process is even more important.

Consider a critical data quality failure during feature generation.

The exact workflow will vary depending on the organization and the risk associated with the application.

The objective is to ensure that technical alerts lead to clear actions.

After all, an alert that nobody owns is just another notification waiting to be ignored.

So far, we've discussed why data quality, lineage, and accountability matter.

But how can we bring these concepts into everyday engineering practices?

Here are five controls that teams can introduce without redesigning their entire architecture.

Data contracts define expectations between data producers and consumers.

They can document schemas, field definitions, units, freshness requirements, and compatibility expectations.

For example, rather than specifying only that annual_income is numeric, a contract should clarify whether it represents gross or net income, the currency, and the applicable time period.

This reduces the risk of downstream systems misinterpreting technically valid information.

Quality gates validate critical data before it progresses through the pipeline.

These checks can be implemented during ingestion, transformation, feature generation, or inference.

For example, a feature engineering process calculating debt-to-income ratios should verify that debt and income values use compatible time periods.

Failure handling should reflect the severity of the issue. Some records may be quarantined, while more serious failures may require stopping the pipeline.

Pipeline execution should produce sufficient metadata to identify source datasets, transformations, and downstream outputs.

Where appropriate, teams should also capture model and feature versions associated with predictions.

This information supports impact analysis, debugging, and investigation when unexpected results occur.

Datasets change, transformation logic is updated, features are modified, and models are retrained.

Versioning helps engineering teams understand which components were active at a particular point in time.

Relevant evidence may include pipeline configurations, dataset snapshots, model versions, validation outcomes, and deployment records.

Every critical data element or pipeline component should have an identified owner or responsible team.

More importantly, ownership should connect directly to incident management and change approval processes.

If a source definition changes, teams should know who evaluates the impact.

If a quality gate fails, the responsible team should receive the alert.

If model performance deteriorates, the investigation should have a clear escalation path.

These controls are most effective when they become part of normal development and deployment practices rather than separate administrative activities.

Implementing comprehensive governance across an entire data environment can be challenging, particularly for organizations with legacy systems and complex dependencies.

A more effective approach is to begin with one critical AI pipeline.

For example, a team operating a loan risk model could start by identifying the inputs that have the greatest influence on its predictions.

These might include income, outstanding debt, repayment history, and credit utilization.

For each critical input, the team can document five things:

Once these foundations are established, the team can implement automated checks and gradually extend the approach to additional datasets.

This incremental strategy also makes it easier to demonstrate the value of governance controls.

For instance, teams can track how quickly data-related incidents are detected, how long investigations take, and whether recurring issues are reduced.

The goal isn't to introduce governance for its own sake.

It's to improve the reliability, maintainability, and transparency of the systems developers are responsible for operating.

Explainable AI has become an important topic in machine learning.

Techniques such as feature importance analysis and SHAP can help teams understand which inputs influence model predictions.

However, explainability and data trustworthiness address different problems.

Suppose a model explanation identifies debt-to-income ratio as a major contributor to a customer's high-risk classification.

That explanation may accurately describe the model's behavior.

But if the debt-to-income ratio was calculated using an incorrectly defined income field, the explanation alone may not reveal the underlying data issue.

This highlights the importance of evaluating AI systems across multiple dimensions.

Model explainability helps us understand how predictions are generated.

Data quality helps establish whether inputs satisfy defined expectations.

Data lineage provides visibility into where information originated and how it was transformed.

Accountability ensures that identified problems can be investigated and addressed.

These capabilities are complementary rather than interchangeable.

None independently guarantees that an AI system is accurate, fair, secure, or compliant. Together, however, they provide a stronger foundation for evaluating and improving system reliability.

As AI systems become more integrated into business processes, engineering teams face increasing expectations around reliability, transparency, and accountability.

Model accuracy and operational performance remain essential, but they represent only part of the overall picture.

A pipeline can execute successfully while processing inconsistent information. A model can generate predictions using features whose definitions have changed. And an explanation can describe a model's behavior without identifying problems in the underlying data.

Building trustworthy AI therefore requires attention to the entire data lifecycle.

Data quality controls help detect unreliable inputs. Lineage provides visibility into how information moves through systems. Clear ownership ensures that issues can be investigated and resolved.

Importantly, these practices don't need to begin with large-scale governance programs or expensive technology investments.

Engineering teams can start with a single critical pipeline, identify its most important data elements, establish quality expectations, and introduce basic traceability and accountability mechanisms.

Over time, these practices can become part of standard development and deployment workflows.

The real measure of a trustworthy AI pipeline isn't simply whether it produces a prediction. It's whether the organization can understand, validate, and take responsibility for the information behind that prediction.

After all, a green dashboard is reassuring. But it shouldn't be the only evidence that an AI system is working as intended.

There is an embarrassment of riches if you're looking to upgrade to a Wi-Fi 7 router for Black Friday

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mesh routers are among the hottest-selling types of routers in networking, and leading the charge are products based on the Wi-Fi 7 standard. Mesh routers enable you to fully cover your home or office with wireless coverage that would otherwise be impossible with a single, standalone router.

Fortunately, numerous manufacturers are producing Wi-Fi 7 mesh routers, offering a wide range of options to choose from. If you prefer seamless integration with your Amazon account and Alexa services, consider opting for the Eero Pro 7. If you want endless configuration options and no-cost features, such as extensive Parental Controls, the Asus ZenWiFi BT4 has you covered. If you're looking for a delicate balance of performance and features at a bargain price, consider the TP-Link Deco BE95.

However, one thing to keep in mind when shopping for a network upgrade is that not all Wi-Fi 7 routers are created equal. While there are speed differences between products that depend on several factors (channel width, total number of streams, etc.), the primary differentiator among Wi-Fi 7 routers comes down to the number of supported bands. There are dual- and tri-band routers, with the latter offering the best potential performance. Dual-band routers only support the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands, while tri-band routers support the higher-performing and shorter-range 6 GHz band. The maximum performance of the 6 GHz band is what gives tri-band Wi-Fi 7 routers a significant theoretical speed advantage over their Wi-Fi 6E predecessors.

Some manufacturers, such as Asus, also offer quad-band routers that feature either two 5 GHz wireless bands or two 6 GHz bands.

With that said, check out the extensive list below for all the best deals on Wi-Fi 7 routers from Asus, Eero, Netgear, MSI, and TP-Link.

The Asus ZenWiFi BD4 is an entry-level Wi-Fi 7 router and thus only supports two bands (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz). This 3-pack features up to 3.6 Gbps of combined throughput and covers 6,500 square feet.

The Deco BE23 is TP-Link's most entry-level Wi-Fi 7 router, sporting dual-band wireless, up to 3.6 Gbps throughput, and coverage of 4,500 square feet.

The Deco BE63 is a mid-range, tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router with four 2.5 GbE ports, 10 Gbps of combined throughput, and coverage of 5,800 square feet.

The TP-Link Deco 7 Pro BE10000 is a tri-band, Wi-Fi 7 mesh system that includes three wireless nodes. Each node comes with four 2.5 GbE ports, and the total wireless coverage is 7,600 square feet.

TP-Link's flagship Deco BE95 Wi-Fi 7 mesh router supports four bands, delivering up to 33 Gbps of throughput. It also features two 10 GbE ports per node.

The Eero Pro 7 is a mid-range, tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router that offers coverage of up to 4,000 square feet. Each wireless node features two 5 GbE ports.

The Eero Max 7 is Amazon's flagship Wi-Fi 7 router, featuring tri-band wireless, two 2.5 GbE ports, two 10 GbE ports, and up to 5,000 square feet of coverage.

The Orbi 770 is the latest in Netgear's long line of Orbi mesh routers. This one is a tri-band system with coverage of up to 5,500 square feet and 11 Gbps of combined throughput. You also get three 2.5 GbE ports and one 2.5 GbE port for WAN.

MSI's Roamii BE Lite is a newcomer on the Wi-Fi 7 mesh router scene, and it's a dual-band unit. Each node includes 2.5 GbE ports, and MSI even provides wall mounts in the box.

The MSI Roamii BE Pro is a high-powered, tri-band Wi-Fi 7 mesh router that won't break the bank. Each node includes four 2.5 GbE ports for connecting your wired devices, and the mesh system is controlled by a rather feature-packed smartphone app.

If you want a high-performance mesh router, look no further. The Asus ZenWiFi BE30000 is a quad-band solution, featuring three wireless nodes. Aggregate speeds across all four bands (you get two 6 GHz bands, one of which is dedicated to a wireless backhaul) are 30 Gbps, and you get coverage for up to 11,000 square feet.

#10271. A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences

User interactions with agents today are where computers were in the terminal era: capable, and answering almost everything in text. Users can ask an agent for anything by typing or talking, and what comes back is usually a wall of text, a poor way to compare three products or edit and approve a detailed plan.

Today, we're releasing A2UI 1.0, the first stable version of our open protocol for generative UI. It lets AI agents answer with interactive screens, such as a form to confirm or a chart. Developers can use it now with open-source renderer SDKs for the web, Android, and iOS and agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. Companies such as Atlassian, Alation, Bloomberg, and ByteDance are already building with it.

With A2UI, the agent describes what to show, and every app draws the UI with its own native components. The application receives A2UI messages and each app renders the content securely and at native speed. Users get the same low latency, high trust, and complete native fidelity whether they reach a company's agent in its own app or in a third-party AI assistant that hosts MCP apps, such as Gemini or Claude.

You wake up sick. Getting through the morning takes six apps: book a video visit, move your meetings, tell your team, turn on an out-of-office reply, ask your partner to do school pickup and order soup. Ask a text-only agent instead, and you get a numbered wall of text, then round after round of “which ones?”. A2UI won't handle your sick day, but it gives developers the framework to build an agent that can. That agent could answer with one view of all six apps. Changing your plan is a couple of taps instead of another round of messages, and nothing is sent until you confirm.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

The same agent output works on any screen. Ask an agent to “move dinner with Priya to Friday”, and it can answer with one view that lines up your calendar, open tables from a restaurant booking app and prices from a rideshare app, so the time that works for everyone is obvious. The developer builds that view once with A2UI, and it renders natively on your phone and on your laptop.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

In both examples, A2UI is the framework that simplifies building these experiences across platforms. Developers build the agent and choose the platforms it works with. A2UI gives them the protocol the agent uses to describe each view, a way to combine components from different apps in one view, and renderers that draw it natively on the web, Android, and iOS.

New to A2UI? Start with the A2UI Playground by CopilotKit or check out industry examples.

Atlassian is bringing A2UI to Jira, where teams can assign work items to AI agents. When an agent needs a follow-up from the team to finish a work item, such as a missing detail or a decision, it asks with an interactive card in the work item, and the team answers right there in Jira.

The Alation Intelligence Operating System (AIOS) builds its feeds using A2UI: metric cards, charts, and more. Each chart can show the SQL query and data behind it. Ask Claude for a feed about profitable products, and the feed renders in the conversation using A2UI to render metric cards, charts, and custom components. The same feed with the same information can be viewed directly inside Alation with a nearly identical layout.

ByteDance released an A2UI renderer for Lynx, its cross-platform framework, in June 2026. Lynx keeps streamed screens smooth and ships a default set of components built on its `lynx-ui` library. In the Lynx GenUI Playground, you can watch A2UI messages rendered natively, for example, as a two-day trip planner for Kyoto. Lynx supports A2UI 0.9 today and is adapting to 1.0 with the A2UI team.

Ask Gemini Notebook for a slide deck and it replies with a card that asks two things: presenter slides or a detailed deck, and which topics to focus on. A review card follows with the format, focus, and visual style, which you can edit before it generates the deck. The same cards guide Video Overviews on the web and on mobile.

Organizations can register their own agents that respond with A2UI. Gemini renders those responses using the components in its A2UI component gallery, and supports A2UI 0.9.1 today. The Google Cloud documentation covers registering an agent and hosting one on Cloud Run.

Several other Google teams, including some behind our largest products, are building features with A2UI.

Several other Google teams, including some behind our largest products, are building features with A2UI that haven’t launched yet. We’ll share more as they ship.

A2UI and MCP Apps work together. Alation already uses both to show its A2UI feeds in Claude. Our June post, A2UI + MCP Apps, covers three ways to combine them, and the A2UI in MCP Apps guide shows how to run A2UI screens inside an MCP App.

Jetpack Compose support for 1.0 is coming soon. Agents in Gemini Enterprise can already use A2UI, and we're working on upgrading Gemini Enterprise to A2UI 1.0. The A2UI roadmap covers the rest, from design-system primitives that render natively on every platform to official SDK support for decision models like Jev.

We’ve collaborated with partners who have built A2UI 1.0 demos across different industries to give you inspiration on how to adapt A2UI to your use cases. Explore what they’ve built:

From Files to Cited Answers in One API Call: Managed Ingestion and SearchDocuments in Agent Retrieval

Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Tunix and Gemma 4 on Google TPUs

Securing Your Agents: A Hands-On Guide to Agent Anomaly Detection

Did the user ask for this? Securing AI agents against intent hijacking with Semantic governance policies

Walmart has the ABS Cyclone M Aqua on sale for just $750, which is a prebuilt that packs an RTX 5060, Core i5-14400F, 16GB of DDR4 memory, and a 1TB SSD. ABS is Newegg's in-house PC brand, and yet Walmart is the only retailer where we found this deal.

Just about any gaming PC you find under $1,000 has some serious compromises given the ongoing RAM, SSD, and GPU pricing crisis's. And this machine too has compromises, notably with the mATX motherboard and single 16GB DDR4-3200 DIMM. You're getting a lot for the money even with those compromises between the Core i5-14400F and RTX 5060, however. As you can see from our roundup of the best Black Friday gaming PC deals, there aren't a ton of options at this price. The ABS Cyclone M Aqua is an mATX prebuilt with an RTX 5060, Core i5-14400F, 16GB of DDR4, and a 1TB NVMe SSD.

As you can see from the data from our GPU benchmark hierarchy, the RTX 5060 is a graphics card that's most comfortable at 1080p, though it can scale up to 1440p, assuming you're willing to lean into Nvidia's DLSS suite between Super Resolution and Multi-Frame Generation, both of which are supported on this GPU.

Its main limitation is the 8GB frame buffer, which could pose issues in some titles at 1440p. For the vast majority of 1080p games, it shouldn't be a problem. In our testing of DLSS 5, which is supported on the RTX 5060, we found that the 8GB frame buffer posed a limitation on performance. However, Nvidia has already apparently slashed the VRAM usage of its DLSS 5 model. The RTX 5060 was fast enough to reach 58 FPS at 1080p with DLSS 5 still.

Outside of the GPU, the Core i5-14400F is the perfect CPU for a rig like this. It provides performance on the level of the Core i5-14600K in games while sacrificing a bit of peak productivity power and the unlocked multiplier.

The one major downside with this configuration is the single 16GB DDR4-3200 DIMM. With just a single stick, your bandwidth is cut in half. Thankfully, the motherboard has four DIMM slots, so you can add another 16GB module to double your capacity and unlock the full bandwidth. Thankfully, DDR4 is much cheaper than DDR5, as you can see in our RAM price tracker.

#10266. Motorola Signature 27 delivery dates slip ahead of launch as it expands to more regions

Motorola and Best Buy websites are now showing an early December shipping date, despite at least one customer already receiving tracking info.

Tons of excitement surrounds Motorola’s upcoming release of the Signature 27, and now retail websites are showing that new preorders won’t be arriving until early December. The original announcement in early November proclaimed a November 19 release date, but Motorola tells 9to5Google:

We’re excited by the strong consumer response of the new motorola signature 27, with demand exceeding our initial expectations. As a result, some orders may experience updated shipping timelines. Our teams are working to meet demand and get devices to customers as quickly as possible.

Motorola and Best Buy websites are still showing “Pre-order” buttons, so while you can order one right now, December 8 and December 11 are the current ship dates. Motorola also just announced that the Motorola Signature 27 will be officially available in India starting December 9 (via GSMArena), further complicating the supply chain.

Despite this, one Redditor who preordered says they received a tracking number for the Signature 27 and the free Motorola Watch Ultra preorder, and it’s scheduled to arrive on November 25. The Motorola Signature 27 has been available in Europe since November 16, so it’s clear demand is quite high for Motorola’s biggest premium launch in a long time.

The Motorola Signature 27 is the most premium phone Motorola has possibly ever launched in North America. The company has shied away from releasing flagship phones here for years, although Motorola’s Razr line of foldable phones often blends premium specs with more mid-range ones. The excitement for the Signature 27 is completely understandable in this case, especially now that Motorola is offering the full seven-year software update treatment that Samsung and Google do.

The Keychron K10 HE keyboard is on sale for $115.99, which is back at the lowest price we've seen it on Amazon. This is a full-size gaming board with a wood frame on the side, along with backlit RGB keys. The RGB is a little less OTT than other models, though, instead going for a classic, rather understated design. It's a magnetic board, too, with magnetic hot-swappable switches.

Jump into the future of keyboards on the cheap (for Hall Effect) with the Keychron K10 HE full-size keyboard. Priced at $115.99, you'd be hard-pressed to find a better deal on full-size Hall Effect keyboard.

You're getting double-shot PBT keycaps here, and underneath them are Gateron double-rail magnetic switches. These give you a lightening-fast response time with a 0.1mm press sensitivity, along with adjustable actuation points for per-key customization. This gives you full flexibility over the entire board.

You've got two options on sale, with the all-black and all-white options at the same $115.99 price: a great deal on a full-size Hall effect keyboard. — Ben Stockton

Anker has carved a name for itself in the portable power bank business, and it's a familiar option for Amazon buyers. Right now, you can pick up its laptop power bank, with a huge 25,000 mAh battery capacity, for just $91.19. That's a 32% discount compared to its usual list price.

The Anker Laptop Power Bank can supply up to 165 watts when two USB-C ports are in use. It also features a retractable USB-C cable and another integrated cable that doubles as a carrying strap.

$91 is enough to get you a power bank with three USB-C ports, including one retractable cable, each capable of 100W each, with a USB-A port capable of 33W. If you're using more than one USB-C cable, you can output a maximum of 165W between them or 133W if you’re using one USB-C port and the USB-A port. If you max out the power bank by using all four ports simultaneously, you’re limited to 130 watts maximum output.

This will let you power up a smartphone, laptop, portable game console, and more, with up to 100W each to supported devices. If your laptop can push that far, it'll carry on charging your laptop until it depletes. It's also capable of charging up itself with a 100W-charger, gaining 30% in 22 minutes.

There's also a built-in display that lets you see charge, device temperature and battery health. If you're on-the-go with plenty of devices in your bag, this is the kind of battery pack you'll want at your disposal. — Ben Stockton

Our favorite gaming chair isn't a typical racing-style chair, but it's not an office one, either. It's this collab between Herman Miller and Logitech G. The Vantum, ergonomic but "built for gamers" with gaming features like an adjustable neckrest, lumbar support and forward-leaning alignment is on sale right now for $768.07 right now, down from $1,155, with an extra 5% off thanks to a Black Friday promo code.

Features an "active, forward leaning alignment," adjustable lumbar support, and passively-adaptive thoracic support. It has a foam-padded seat cushion and a mesh suspension backrest for breathability, as well as an adjustable neck rest.

The Vantum is a seriously premium chair. It has a mesh backrest and a padded cushioned seat, along with 4D armrests with padding. As you can imagine, it scored well in our Herman Miller x Logitech G Vantum review, thanks to its lightweight but comfortable design, with the adjustable lumbar support similar to the functionality you'd see in the company's pricier Herman Miller task chairs.

While the chair doesn't offer full recline, its tilt mechanism is pretty comfortable, as is the passively-adaptive thoracic support. This Black Friday discount means you can save $386.93, as long as you use the SAVE5 code at checkout to get the full discount. — Ben Stockton

The Logitech Yeti Orb is the spiritual successor to the classic Blue Snowball microphone — it's a unique-looking, ball-shaped microphone that sits on top of a sturdy desktop tripod stand and sounds great out of the box. It's our favorite budget-priced gaming mic and it's on sale right now for an even more budget-friendly $39.99 at Best Buy — $30 off its MSRP of $69.99.

This round, ball-shaped desktop mic features a cardioid polar pattern and sounds great out of the box. It comes with a desktop stand and has customizable RGB lighting, and can be mounted at two different angles.

The Yeti Orb is a simple, stylish microphone that comes with a plastic desktop tripod stand in the box. It has the Blue Snowball's iconic ball shape, with two mounting points — so you can mount it straight on, or at an angle, depending on whether you're mounting it on the included stand or on a boom arm. There are no on-mic controls or ports (other than its USB-C port), so you won't be able to adjust the mic's gain or plug in a headset for zero-latency monitoring, and for that reason it's not really a mic for serious streamers. But it does have customizable RGB lighting, which indicates whether the mic is recording, and it sounds great right out of the box — so while you can tweak the settings using Logitech G Hub (which comes with Blue Vo!ce), you don't have to. It's a great mic for casual chatting and streaming, and this is a great price to get it at. You can read my full review of the Logitech Yeti Orb here. — Sarah

Corsair's wireless MMO / MOBA-focused gaming mouse features 16 programmable buttons, including 12 in a side array, and sports Corsair's 33K Marksman S optical sensor. It also has native integration with Elgato's Stream Deck platform, so you can map Stream Deck commands directly to the buttons.

If you're looking for a mouse with tons of buttons, look no further than Corsair's Scimitar line — the Corsair Scimitar Elite SE Wireless is currently on sale for just $69.99 at Best Buy, which is 50% off its retail price of $139.99. And if you don't need a wireless mouse, the wired Corsair Scimitar RGB Elite is down to $49.99 at Amazon, which is 44% off its retail price of $89.99.

The Scimitar RGB Elite mouse from Corsair features 17 programmable buttons, including 12 located on the side panel, the left/right primary mouse buttons, two DPI switch buttons above the scroll wheel, and the scroll wheel's center click. You can slide the 12-button side panel to fit your hand size.

The Corsair Scimitar Elite SE Wireless is an MMO / MOBA-focused gaming mouse with an adjustable 12-button side panel — it doesn't swap out, like the side panel on the Razer Naga V2 / V3 Pro, but it does move forward and back (it comes with a hex tool so you can adjust it to where you want and lock it in). It doesn't move a ton, but it's a nice accommodation for people who find that the giant gaming mice that dominate the market don't have buttons in quite the right places.

The Scimitar Elite SE Wireless sports Corsair's Marksman S 33K sensor, which has a maximum resolution of 33,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 750 IPS and can handle up to 50 G's of force. It's a heavier mouse — 4.02oz / 114g, but weight isn't that big of a deal in the MMO / MOBA community. Also, it's integrated with Elgato's Stream Deck platform, so you can program Stream Deck functionality directly to the mouse's buttons. You can read my full review of the Corsair Scimitar Elite SE Wireless here. — Sarah

The 9800X3D might not be the fastest gaming CPU on the market but it's still the best option owing to its speed and power draw. Now, at Amazon, it just crashed to an all-time low of $369, thanks to a coupon you can apply before checking out.

The Ryzen 7 9800X3D is a potent gaming 8-core, 16-thread desktop CPU. It has a massive 96MB L3 cache for gaming performance, with clock speeds of up to 5.2GHz.

The 9800X3D really needs no introduction, but in case you aren't familiar, this is one the best gaming CPUs around. IT isn't quite AMD's fastest — the 9850X3D takes that crown — but this chip draws significantly less power while still being very close in terms of performance. The industry leading 3D V-Cache means the CPU is much less reliant on your slower RAM, drastically boosting frame rates.

This deal is not likely to be around for long, so move fast if you want one to start an AM5 build or upgrade your existing rig. - Stephen Warwick

This TKL mechanical keyboard features hot-swappable switches and a built-in Stream Deck with 12 LCD keys, a 2.75-inch screen, and 2 rotary knobs.

The Corsair Galleon 100 SD is a keyboard with an integrated Stream Deck — it's a mechanical keyboard with a TKL layout, plus a 2-knob, 12-key Stream Deck that has all the functionality of Elgato's Stream Deck platform. Although I still lament the lack of a true 10-key numberpad, I have to admit that the Corsair Galleon 100 SD has been my daily driver for the better part of the past year. Who knew an integrated Stream Deck was so useful?!

Of course, at $350... it's definitely not cheap. But right now it's down to $259.99 at Best Buy — $90 off its retail price, and a pretty good deal when you consider you're getting both a keyboard and a Stream Deck in one.

The Galleon 100 SD is a pretty premium keyboard, with a nice-looking design, double-shot PBT keycaps, a pass-through USB port, and a hot-swappable PCB. It comes with only one switch option: Corsair's MLX Pulse (purple) switches, which are "thocky and linear" — and they sound pretty good, though they're definitely linear. The case has six layers of sound-dampening foam and it's a great-sounding keyboard overall, especially for a mainstream gaming keyboard.

The Stream Deck features 12 LCD keys that are the same size and shape as typical Stream Deck keys. There's a 2.75-inch LCD screen above the keys, which is divided into quadrants that are controlled by the two notched, clickable rotary knobs at the top. The Stream Deck is a true Stream Deck, so it has all the functionality of Elgato's platform, and can be easily programmed with the Stream Deck software. The keyboard also comes with a soft-touch plastic wrist rest, two USB cables, and a handful of other accessories in the box. You can read my full review of the Corsair Galleon 100 SD here. — Sarah

The Turtle Beach Atlas Air lives up to its name — this wireless, open-back headset is lightweight and airy in both comfort and sound. Although its all-plastic design didn't feel quite up to the $179.99 price point it debuted at, the comfort and audio quality was enough for us to recommend it — and now it's down to just $119.99 at Amazon for Black Friday.

The only wireless open-back gaming headset on the market is incredibly light and comfortable and sounds great. It has a detachable, flip-to-mute boom mic, dual-mode wireless connectivity, and gets about 50 hours of battery life.

The Atlas Air is a wireless, open-back headset, which means the sound isn't closed in. While this does mean that people around you can hear what you're listening to, there are several benefits to an open-back design — specifically, you don't get the same listening fatigue you get when listening to a closed-back headset, because the sound can escape instead of reverberating inside your head. For gamers, it also allows for a wider soundstage and a more immersive environment. As long as you don't work in close quarters, an open-back headset is a nice option if you don't want to commit to speakers.

The Atlas Air has a lightweight, plastic build, with a mesh suspension headband and floating earcups. It's extremely lightweight — just 10.61oz / 301g — and it basically feels like you're wearing nothing. It sports 40mm dynamic drivers with a frequency response range of 20 - 40,000 Hz, and it sounds surprisingly good: it has a nice, wide soundstage and a slightly bass-heavy sound profile, and it did especially well with picking up details in layered audio environments, such as cities and jungles. It's probably not the headset for those looking to gain advantage in shooting games — the directional sound is fine, but a closed-back headset will help you zero in on footsteps and gunshots. But for the less competitive games, this is a great option, especially if you find other headsets hard to wear for long periods of time. You can read my full review of the Atlas Air here. — Sarah

The Razer Naga V2 Pro is one of my favorite mice of all time, because I can never have enough buttons on a mouse. This wireless mouse is aimed at MMO / MOBA players, but it can actually be used by just about anyone thanks to the three swappable side plates it comes bundled with. Naturally, this kind of versatility doesn't come cheap, but right now you can grab the Naga V2 Pro for just $129.99 at Amazon — $50 off its MSRP of $179.99.

The Razer Naga V2 Pro sports a customizable magnetic side plate, offering 12-, 6-, and 2-button configurations, Razer's Hyperscroll Pro wheel, fully wireless connectivity, and its Focus Pro 30K Optical sensor.

The Naga V2 Pro comes with three interchangeable side plates with 12-, 6-, and 2-button configurations. It's not the lightest mouse on the market — it weighs 4.72oz / 134g, but lightness is not what most MMO players are looking for. Instead, they're looking for comfort, and the Naga V2 Pro is a very comfortable mouse, with a contoured, ergonomic right-handed shape and a rest for your ring finger. It sports Razer's Focus Pro 30K optical sensor, which has a maximum sensitivity of 30,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 750 IPS and can handle up to 70 G's of acceleration. It also has a customizable tilt wheel, which can be tuned in Razer's Synapse software.

I used this mouse for two years straight, until I recently replaced it with the Razer Naga V3 Pro — more because my Naga V2 Pro was starting to look a little worse for the wear, not because it wasn't still a fantastic mouse. You can read my full review of the Razer Naga V2 Pro here. — Sarah

The HyperX Cloud III wired gaming headset is one of the most comfortable headsets we've ever tested — it's almost exactly the same as the HyperX Cloud III S Wireless, just, well, wired. It has a premium build with a steel headband and curved aluminum forks, large over-ear earcups with leatherette-covered memory foam padding, and a leatherette-covered padded headband. It's sleek and understated, with a detachable boom microphone, and it's fairly lightweight at just 10.86oz / 308g. And it's currently on sale for $39 at Walmart — down $60.99 from its MSRP of $99.99.

The HyperX Cloud III is a wired gaming headset with a detachable microphone. It features 53mm drivers and virtual surround sound support.

The Cloud III wired gaming headset is basically the most comfortable headset we've tested in recent years. It's fairly adjustable, with earcups that tilt and are independently height-adjustable (they don't pivot, but the forks allow for some lateral movement and the headband is very flexible). The memory foam padding is thick and soft enough to wear comfortably over glasses, and the clamping force is practically perfect — enough that it won't fall off if you tilt your head back, but not much stronger than that. Add this into the weight and you have a headset that you can wear for hours and hours at a time without needing a break.

The headset sports HyperX's angled 53mm dynamic drivers, which have a frequency response range of 10 - 21,000 Hz — slightly outside the typical frequency response range of most gaming headsets, and nicely tuned to give you a neutral audio profile that still brings plenty of bass. This is the wired version, and it comes with an analog cable that can plug into a USB cable extension, which gives you plenty of length for when you're sitting at a PC while still being able to plug into any standard 3.5mm jack. It was already a good deal at its starting $100 price point, and at $39 it's absolutely worth it.

You can read my full review of the HyperX Cloud III wired gaming headset here. — Sarah

The quirky G3S case from Wokyis might be pushing the limits of practicality (not to mention copyright infringement), but it sure is cute and nostalgic. It’s a plastic shell that tips your Mac Mini (M6, M5 Pro, and M4 models) on its side and turns it into a tiny Power Mac G3 tower.

Whether you were a Mac fan in the late 90s or not, there’s a whole lot of nostalgia in this design. It’s available in four colors and is currently 50% off, taking it down to $19.99 at Amazon.

This ABS plastic Mac Mini case is pure nostalgia and not all that practical, but there are benefits to tipping Apple’s smallest Mac up on its side.

Aside from the throwback 90s looks, tipping the Mac Mini on its side like this actually lets you press the power button without lifting up the mini PC. Plus, if your desk space is cramped, putting the system on its side will free up some room. -- Matt Safford

If you're in the market for a current-gen RTX 50-series card that won't set you back thousands of dollars, then this might be the deal for you. Newegg is selling the cheapest RTX 5060 you can buy right now at $439.99, an $80 saving. While that's a far cry from the MSRP of $299, GPUs are very expensive these days, so this is about as good as it gets for 1080p gaming.

Get an RTX 5060 with 8GB of GDDR7 VRAM, clock speeds of 2550 MHz, 3840 CUDA cores, and a free GPU holder.

At 1080p, the RTX 5060 can put out more than 60 fps, making it perfect for entry-level gaming. It also supports Nvidia's DLSS technologies, so you can squeeze out more frames or even try your hand at 1440p.

This specific version of the RTX 5060 is Zotac's AMP series, with core clocks of 2550 MHz, with the same speed listed for its boost clocks. It has 3840 CUDA cores, and 8GB of GDDR7 VRAM with a 128-bit memory interface. While this won't blow titles out of the water at 4K, this is budget gaming performance at a time when GPUs are becoming increasingly more expensive. - Stephen Warwick

Buying a PC on Black Friday doesn't have to mean spending the Earth. If you want a budget build, this Intel Core i7 14700F rig from Cyberpower is a fantastic cheap option for 1080p gaming. With an RTX 5060 Ti 8GB, this should be brilliant for entry-level gaming and could even be pushed to 1440p with Nvidia's DLSS technology.

The CyberPower Gamer Xtreme prebuilt PC offers a 20-Core Intel i7 14700F CPU, RTX 5060 Ti GPU, 16GB of DDR5 memory, and 1 TB of storage, wrapped up in a white case, and flush with glowing RGB fans.

As you can see from our testing data, in our 19-game testing suite, the RTX 5060 Ti 8GB is good for average frame rates of 72 fps. This drops to around 46 at 1440p without any help from frame generation.

The CPU in this build is Intel's i7 14700F with 20 cores and 28 threads, boasting boost clocks of up to 5.4 GHz- a great processor for productivity and gaming.

Aside from the potent 20-core CPU and GPU for 1080, you also get 16GB of DDR5 RAM and a 1TB SSD. Windows 11 Home comes as standard, and the motherboard supports Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.3. There are also ports aplenty. - Stephen Warwick

Samsung's P9 Express microSDXC is one of the top storage solutions for Nintendo Switch 2. With transfer speeds of up to 800 MB/s and similar sequential read speeds, this is a speedy storage solution for your handheld.

The Switch 2 ships with 256GB of internal storage as standard, so a 512GB expansion will triple that capacity for storing games and files. While not quite its lowest-ever price, there's a great deal on this card, 38% off at Amazon, now just $92.99.

The Samsung P9 is a microSD Express card that offers great performance and reliability for its price. The 512GB model is currently priced at its original MSRP of $99.99.

The P9 Express comes with Dynamic Thermal Guard technology to stop your card from overheating while in use for smoother gameplay. It also has a three-year warranty and can be used with microSD UHS-I devices such as tablets and drones, too.

The 256GB model is also on sale, an arguably better value. At 44% off, it's less than half the price of the 512GB model. In theory, buying two would get you the same amount of storage for $89, provided you don't mind swapping cards around.

The Samsung P9 is a microSD Express card that offers great performance and reliability for its price. The 256GB model is currently priced at its original MSRP of $44.99.

With SSD and flash storage prices through the roof thanks to AI, this is a solid deal on a great Nintendo Switch 2 card. - Stephen Warwick

I use the Gateron Oil King Ghost Pro switches on my own keyboard, and they're a go-to linear switch for a good reason. The heavier 50gf operating force is heavier than a standard Red-style switch, leading to a deep sound and more pronounced feedback while typing, particularly if you're a heavy typer.

The Oil King Ghost Pro switches are linear key switches for a mechanical keyboard with a 50gf operating force.

These switches are an upgraded version of standard Oil Kings, with the new Ghost name noting the passthrough channel for lighting. The switches themselves are the same, and they come factory lubricated, so they sound great out of the box. You can use the switches with any standard 3-pin or 5-pin PCB — Jake Roach

This hefty Lenovo Legion gaming laptop is the first RTX 5090-powered laptop we've seen under $4,000. This is a huge spec with a 240Hz OLED display, 24GB VRAM GPU, a massive 24-core Intel Core Ultra 9 290HX CPU, 32GB of DDR5 RAM, and a 1TB SSD.

The 16-inch Lenovo Legion Pro 7i gaming laptop comes with an Intel Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus CPU, RTX 5090 (175W TGP) GPU, 32GB of DDR5 memory, and 1TB of storage. The OLED display offers a 240Hz refresh rate and a 2560 x 1600 resolution.

With its 24 cores and performance core boost clocks of up to 5.5 GHz, this is a fantastic mobile CPU for both work and play. Combined with the laptop RTX 5090, the best laptop GPU on the market, this will make light work of any title you can throw at it in the 2560 x 1200 resolution. That stunning OLED will really make games pop, too.

Also offers 1x Thunderbolt 4 port (USB-C), 1x 3.2 Gen 2 (USB-C), 1x USB 3.2 Gen 2 (USB-A), 2x USB 3.2 Gen 1 (USB-A), a 3.5mm headphone jack, 1x HDMI 2.1 port, and a 2.5 Gbps Ethernet jack, as well as Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4. While we haven't reviewed this specific spec, in our Lenovo Legion Pro 7i Gen 10 review, the laptop scored very well thanks to its exceptional OLED screen, aluminum chassis, and sharp webcam. - Stephen Warwick

Earlier this week, we highlighted a great deal on Apple's MacBook Neo, which is $100 off and back to its original launch price of $599. This is also better than the previous $50 discount to $649, so if you missed out the first time, this deal is now better! The $599 price gets you 256GB of storage and 8GB of RAM, and is available in all four of Apple's vibrant colors.

You can also snag the 512GB version for $699, a $100 discount.

Apple's base MacBook Neo has an A18 Pro chip, 256GB of storage, and 8GB of RAM. A solid alternative with a more powerful SoC.

The A18 Pro chip in the MacBook Neo is solid for single-core productivity performance excelling in single-core performance, though the 8GB can be difficult for serious multitasking. For people working on basic tasks, this is going to be sufficient.There have been a handful of other deals on the Neo so far this week. We saw the base model drop to $599 (in citrus only) at one point, while the upgraded 512GB model with Touch ID dropped to $699 (in blush) at another. It's possible we'll see more color-specific price drops, but it's not a guarantee, and $649 isn't bad given the RAM situation. — Andrew E. Freedman

In what might be one of the best gaming PC deals we've seen so far, this HyperX OMEN desktop at Best Buy, featuring Intel's Core Ultra 7 270K Plus and RTX 5080 GPU, is now just $2,699. The graphics card in this build alone currently retails for around $1,700, making this a really good value build.

Get an RTX 5080 PC with Intel Core Ultra 7 270K Plus, 16GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD, with plenty of space to upgrade. Also features Wi-Fi 7.

The star of the show here is the RTX 5080, a fully-fledged 4K GPU that will take care of any title you want to play at high resolutions and settings. That's complemented by the Intel Core Ultra 7 270K, a much-improved Intel gaming CPU released not too long ago. With 24 cores, it performs extremely well in productivity tasks as well as gaming. While it can't quite match the X3D SKUs of AMD for gaming performance, it is still a very strong desktop CPU.

The supporting cast of the build is perhaps the only compromise. The 1TB SSD is fine to get you started, but 16GB of RAM is a little less than we'd like in a build of this caliber. Still, this is such a cheap build for an RTX 5080 that it will be worth the trade-off for some. Of course, if you already have some DDR5 RAM lying around, you could swap that in, or you could spend some of that $1,700 saving on an upgrade.

The build supports up to 128GB of memory, with 4 DIMM slots for future expansion. It also has two further SSD slots, as well as Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.0, thanks to the Intel Z890 motherboard inside.

This build will not be around for long, so move fast if you want to grab one. - Stephen Warwick

Whether you need to upgrade your boot drive or you’re attempting to rescue the laptop or gaming PC of a friend or family member, an SSD cloner can make a scary, potentially tedious job surprisingly easy. I know because I bought this cloner a couple of years ago (when it cost about $15 more) and moved someone’s existing OS from an extremely cramped 128GB drive onto a faster 512GB drive in less than half an hour. And now Rosewill’s SSD cloner is on sale for its lowest-ever price at Amazon.

With support for NVMe M.2 SSDs and offline cloning, this handy device makes it simple to move your files or OS from one drive to another. And with a 20 Gbps USB-C interface, it's also speedy in your OS of choice if you want to use software to clone or move your data between drives.

Keep in mind this device only supports M Key PCIe / NVMe drives, so it won’t work with SATA M.2 drives. But it can work both as a standalone drive or with software if you need to, say, resize the partition. The Rosewill cloner is also handy for checking the contents of M.2 drives you may have lying around. But if that's all you need, you can get a good tool-free enclosure for less than $20. -- Matt Safford

Hello and welcome to day two of our Black Friday coverage, Stephen here to see you through the early hours of the morning!
